items.prompt: Why does a cow bring food back up from its stomach to chew it a second time?

options.label: Chewing again breaks tough plant fibre into smaller pieces
options.feedback: Smaller pieces expose more surface for the microbes fermenting the food to work on, speeding digestion.

options.label: It removes poison from the plants she has eaten
options.feedback: Chewing changes the size of a piece of food, not its chemistry. Toxins are not affected by being ground finer.

options.label: It lets her taste the food a second time
options.feedback: Taste buds are near the front of the mouth and play no role in why a cow bothers to re-chew already swallowed food.

options.label: It cools the food before it is swallowed again
options.feedback: Food is already close to body temperature by the time it comes back up. Temperature has nothing to do with this habit.

items.ok_line: A second grinding, so the microbes doing the real work have more to grip.
items.ko_line: Grass is mostly tough fibre. Ask what a second round of chewing does to a fibre that resisted the first bite.
items.exp_title: Grinding fibre down for the microbes
items.exp_text: A cow's first chew is quick and shallow, mostly meant to swallow rather than to fully break the grass down, and the coarse mass then sits in the first stomach chamber where it softens. Later, small balls of it are brought back up and chewed slowly and thoroughly this second time, tearing tough fibre into much finer pieces. Since the plant matter is actually digested by microbes fermenting it rather than by the cow's own teeth, that finer grinding hands those microbes far more surface to attack at once.

items.prompt: Since no mammal makes an enzyme that breaks down cellulose, how do plant-eaters get any nutrition out of tough plant fibre at all?

options.label: Microbes living in their gut ferment it for them
options.feedback: Bacteria and other microbes carry the enzyme the mammal lacks, breaking cellulose apart and releasing usable nutrients as a by-product.

options.label: Their stomach acid dissolves the fibre directly
options.feedback: Acid alone does not break the chemical bonds holding cellulose together. Something with the right enzyme is still needed.

options.label: Their teeth grind it fine enough to digest on their own
options.feedback: Grinding changes the size of the fibre, not the strength of the bonds inside it. Small pieces of cellulose remain just as indigestible as large ones.

options.label: Their body converts the fibre straight into fat
options.feedback: Nothing in a mammal's own body has a means to convert cellulose into anything before it is broken down first, and mammal cells cannot do that breaking down themselves.

items.ok_line: Borrowed enzymes, carried by trillions of tenants in the gut.
items.ko_line: The mammal's own cells never gained the enzyme for this job. Someone else living inside it did.
items.exp_text: Cellulose is built from sugar units locked together by a chemical bond that mammal digestive enzymes cannot open, so on their own, plant-eaters could extract almost nothing from grass or leaves. What they carry instead is a gut swarming with bacteria and other microbes that do produce the right enzyme, and these microbes ferment the fibre, releasing simple compounds the mammal's own gut wall can absorb. The mammal supplies the space and the food; the actual chemistry of digestion is outsourced entirely.

items.prompt: What is actually happening inside a cow's rumen, the first and largest of its stomach chambers?

options.label: Billions of microbes are fermenting the swallowed plant matter
options.feedback: A warm, churning vat where microbes multiply and break fibre down chemically, long before any of it reaches the cow's own digestive juices.

options.label: Stomach acid is dissolving the plant matter
options.feedback: Strong acid appears only in a later chamber. The rumen itself stays close to neutral, exactly what the microbes living there need.

options.label: The food is simply being stored until there is room to swallow more
options.feedback: Storage happens, but it is not idle. Active fermentation is under way the entire time the food sits there.

options.label: Water is being filtered out of the food
options.feedback: Water absorption is handled much further along the gut, in the intestines, not inside the rumen.

items.ok_line: A fermentation vat, not a stomach in the usual sense at all.
items.ko_line: The rumen is closer to neutral than acidic, which is a strong clue about what kind of process is running inside it.
items.exp_title: A fermentation vat before the real stomach
items.exp_text: The rumen holds a huge population of bacteria, fungi and other microbes living in a warm, oxygen-free, near-neutral broth, and it is these microbes, not the cow, that actually break the swallowed plant fibre down through fermentation. The cow's own digestive juices play no part here; they wait in a separate chamber further along, where the fermented mixture, along with a share of the microbes themselves, is finally digested in the ordinary way. In effect, the cow eats grass, but a colony of microbes eats first.

items.prompt: Why does a horse digest grass in a different way from a cow?

options.label: A horse ferments its food in an enlarged pouch near the end of the gut
options.feedback: Food passes through a horse's own stomach first and is fermented only afterward, in a chamber called the cecum.

options.label: A horse has no microbes helping it digest fibre at all
options.feedback: A horse relies on fermenting microbes just as much as a cow does. What differs is where in the gut that fermentation happens.

options.label: A horse's stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve fibre alone
options.feedback: No mammal's stomach acid can break cellulose apart by itself. A horse still depends on microbial fermentation for that.

options.label: A horse chews its food only once and swallows it whole
options.feedback: A horse does thoroughly chew before swallowing. What sets it apart from a cow is not how it chews but where fermentation occurs afterward.

items.ok_line: Fermentation after the stomach, rather than before it.
items.ko_line: Both animals rely on the same trick, microbial fermentation. The question is only where in the gut it happens.
items.exp_title: Fermenting after the stomach, not before
items.exp_text: A cow's stomach comes after its fermentation chamber, so the microbe-broken fibre is digested a second time by the cow's own juices before anything is absorbed. A horse runs the process in the opposite order: grass first passes through an ordinary acidic stomach and small intestine, and only afterward reaches an enlarged pouch called the cecum, where microbes ferment whatever fibre survived that far. Because the fibre meets the horse's own digestion before fermentation rather than after, a horse extracts less total nutrition from the same mouthful of grass than a cow does.

items.prompt: Why are a plant-eating mammal's back teeth broad and ridged rather than pointed?

options.label: A wide, ridged surface grinds fibrous plant matter between two rows of teeth
options.feedback: Ridges catch and shred the fibre as the jaw grinds side to side, doing to plant tissue what a pointed tooth never could.

options.label: They need to look intimidating to predators
options.feedback: Herbivore teeth generally stay hidden inside a closed mouth and play no part in warding off a predator.

options.label: They help the animal produce more saliva
options.feedback: Saliva comes from glands elsewhere in the mouth. Tooth shape has no bearing on how much of it is produced.

options.label: They allow the animal to swallow food whole without chewing
options.feedback: Broad ridged teeth exist precisely because the food is chewed thoroughly before being swallowed, not skipped over.

items.ok_line: A ridged surface built to shred fibre, not to pierce or tear.
items.ko_line: Think about what job a flat, ridged surface does well that a sharp point does not.
items.exp_title: A millstone in place of a blade
items.exp_text: Plant tissue is held together by fibre running through it in every direction, and breaking it apart calls for crushing and shredding rather than a single sharp cut. A herbivore's molars meet this need with broad, flattened surfaces carved into ridges, and as the jaw swings side to side, those ridges on the upper and lower teeth scrape past each other, tearing the fibre apart the way a millstone grinds grain. That grinding motion is also why plant-eaters wear their teeth down far faster than meat-eaters, whose pointed teeth mostly pierce and slice instead of rubbing against each other.

items.prompt: Why is a plant-eating mammal's gut generally much longer than a meat-eater's?

options.label: Plant fibre needs far more time and surface area to break down
options.feedback: Extra length buys extra time for slow microbial fermentation and gives more surface for absorbing what that fermentation releases.

options.label: A longer gut lets a plant-eater eat less often
options.feedback: A plant-eater with a long gut still needs to eat large amounts regularly. Gut length changes how food is processed, not how often eating is needed.

options.label: Plant matter weighs more than meat, needing more space
options.feedback: Space to hold food and the length of gut wall it passes along are two different things. Weight alone does not require extra length.

options.label: A longer gut makes the animal's body more efficient at running
options.feedback: Gut length has no direct bearing on how an animal moves. Its role is entirely about digestion, not locomotion.

items.ok_line: Fibre resists breaking down, so the gut buys time by being long.
items.ko_line: Meat is already close to what a mammal's own enzymes can use directly. Plant fibre is not, and that gap is the clue.
items.exp_title: Length bought for time and surface
items.exp_text: Meat is close in composition to a mammal's own tissue, and a meat-eater's own enzymes can break it down quickly in a short gut. Plant fibre is nothing like that: it resists a mammal's enzymes entirely and can only be unlocked slowly, by microbes fermenting it over hours. A longer gut, or an enlarged chamber built into it, buys the time that slow fermentation needs and offers a much larger surface for absorbing the nutrients it eventually releases.

items.prompt: Why does a rabbit eat its own droppings rather than passing them once and leaving them behind?

options.label: A soft first dropping still carries nutrients its gut missed the first time through
options.feedback: Passed again through the gut, that soft dropping gives a second chance to absorb nutrients that fermentation only finished releasing after the food had already moved on.

options.label: It is simply keeping its burrow clean
options.feedback: A behaviour aimed at hygiene would not involve deliberately eating the material rather than moving it elsewhere.

options.label: It needs the extra bulk to feel full
options.feedback: A rabbit already eats large amounts of plant matter through the day. Feeling full is not what drives this particular habit.

options.label: It is replacing water lost earlier in the day
options.feedback: A dropping is not a significant source of water for a rabbit. What it carries that matters is nutrients, not moisture.

items.ok_line: A second pass through the gut, to catch what fermentation finished too late the first time.
items.ko_line: A rabbit produces two different kinds of droppings, and eats only one of them. Ask what makes that one special.
items.exp_title: A second pass to catch what came too late
items.exp_text: Fermentation inside a rabbit's enlarged cecum finishes releasing many nutrients only after the plant matter has already moved past the point in the gut where absorption normally happens. Rather than losing that food value, the rabbit produces a soft, nutrient-rich dropping from this batch and eats it directly from the body, sending it through the gut a second time so absorption can finally catch up. The dry, crumbly droppings left on the ground are a separate, already-spent batch that gets no second chance.

items.prompt: How does a giraffe manage to browse leaves that no other ground animal in its habitat can reach?

options.label: An unusually long neck lifts its mouth well above the competition
options.feedback: The same seven neck bones every mammal has are simply stretched far longer in a giraffe, raising its head into branches nothing else can browse.

options.label: It can jump higher than other browsing animals
options.feedback: A giraffe's build favours reaching upward while standing, not leaping. Height comes from its neck and legs, not from any jump.

options.label: It pulls branches down with its front legs
options.feedback: Front legs are used for standing and moving, not for grasping and pulling branches, a job the neck and tongue handle instead.

options.label: It knocks leaves loose by shaking the tree
options.feedback: Feeding this way would waste far more leaves than it delivers to the mouth, and it is not how a giraffe actually browses.

items.ok_line: The same number of neck bones as any mammal, just enormously stretched.
items.ko_line: Every mammal, giraffe included, has exactly the same count of bones in its neck. What differs is their length.
items.exp_text: Nearly every mammal, from a mouse to a whale, carries exactly seven bones in its neck, and a giraffe is no exception; each of its seven is simply far longer than in any other animal, stacking up into a neck that can lift its head several metres off the ground. A long, flexible tongue then works branches into its mouth from around thorns that would stop a shorter-necked browser. The height this buys opens up a layer of leaves that grazing animals below never get the chance to touch.

items.prompt: Why must an elephant spend most of its waking hours eating?

options.label: Its gut absorbs only a small share of the fibre that passes through
options.feedback: Because so much of each meal passes through only partly broken down, the elephant makes up for that waste by processing an enormous volume of plant matter instead.

options.label: Its stomach is too small to hold much food at once
options.feedback: An elephant's stomach is large, in keeping with its body. The reason it must eat so much has to do with efficiency, not with capacity.

options.label: Its trunk can only gather small amounts of food at a time
options.feedback: A trunk is a remarkably efficient tool for gathering food quickly. It is not the limiting step in why an elephant eats so long each day.

options.label: It needs to keep its tusks worn down
options.feedback: Tusks do wear from use, but that is a side effect of feeding, not the reason an elephant needs to spend so long doing it.

items.ok_line: A gut that wastes a lot of each meal, made up for by processing a lot of meals.
items.ko_line: Think about how thoroughly the food is actually broken down, rather than how it is gathered or stored.
items.exp_title: Making up in volume what is lost in efficiency
items.exp_text: An elephant relies on fermentation happening late in its gut, in a large cecum, and food moves through fairly quickly, which leaves a substantial share of the fibre in each mouthful still undigested by the time it is passed. Rather than slowing that passage down to extract more from less, an elephant compensates by taking in an enormous volume of plant matter, so that even a low rate of absorption per mouthful adds up to enough. The trunk that plucks branches and grass with such speed exists largely to keep pace with just how much needs to go in.

items.prompt: How does a koala survive on eucalyptus leaves, which are mildly toxic to most other mammals?

options.label: Microbes in its gut break the toxins down before they cause harm
options.feedback: Specialised bacteria living in an enlarged section of its gut neutralise the leaf's chemical defences as the food passes through.

options.label: Its liver has grown large enough to filter out any poison
options.feedback: A koala's liver is not unusually enlarged. The defence against the toxins happens earlier, in the gut, before the blood is ever involved.

options.label: It only eats eucalyptus leaves once they have dried and lost their toxins
options.feedback: A koala feeds mainly on fresh leaves, toxins included. Waiting for them to dry is not part of how it copes with them.

options.label: It builds up immunity to the toxins over its lifetime
options.feedback: Immunity describes how a body responds to threats like infection. A chemical toxin in food is dealt with by breaking it down, not by an immune response.

items.ok_line: Gut microbes doing the detox work before the toxins ever reach the bloodstream.
items.ko_line: As with grass and fibre elsewhere in this chapter, the answer here again lives in the gut, not in an organ further along.
items.exp_text: Eucalyptus leaves are laced with oily compounds that are toxic to most mammals if enough of them reach the bloodstream. A koala carries an unusually long cecum packed with bacteria adapted to break these compounds down chemically while the leaf matter still sits in the gut, well before anything is absorbed into the blood. Because this detoxifying work is so specialised, a koala can barely digest anything else; the same microbes that make eucalyptus safe leave it almost unable to switch to another plant.
